fixtures.name: ml_blog_intro
fixtures.task: Write the intro to my blog post announcing our new method for reducing classifier-free guidance saturation in diffusion models. Audience: ML practitioners.
fixtures.draft:
When classifier-free guidance scales past roughly 7–10, samples from diffusion models stop getting more faithful to the prompt and start collapsing: colors oversaturate, contrast blows out, textures harden into plasticky surfaces, and diverse prompts converge onto a narrow set of compositions. This is the well-known guidance saturation problem, and it's usually blamed on the guided score drifting off the data manifold — the extrapolation between conditional and unconditional predictions grows linearly with the guidance weight, but the region where that extrapolation stays close to a real image does not.

We propose [METHOD NAME], a drop-in modification to the CFG update that keeps the guided prediction inside a learned trust region around the conditional score. The change is roughly ten lines of sampler code, adds no training, and costs one extra norm computation per step.

The rest of the post walks through (1) a diagnostic showing where standard CFG leaves the manifold, measured via conditional score norms across timesteps; (2) the derivation of the trust-region update and its relationship to prior fixes like CFG++ and dynamic thresholding; (3) FID, CLIP-score, and diversity numbers on SD 1.5, SDXL, and a class-conditional ImageNet DiT, with ablations over the trust-region radius in the final table; and (4) failure cases, including prompts where the method underguides.

fixtures.name: physics_abstract
fixtures.task: Draft an abstract for my paper reporting anomalous thermal conductivity measurements in twisted bilayer graphene at the magic angle.
fixtures.draft: We report thermal conductivity measurements of twisted bilayer graphene at the magic angle (1.1°) from 10 K to 300 K using suspended microbridge thermometry. Near charge neutrality, the in-plane thermal conductivity is suppressed by a factor of 6.2 at 50 K relative to Bernal-stacked bilayer graphene, with the suppression persisting but weakening to a factor of 2.1 at 300 K. The electronic contribution, extracted via the Wiedemann-Franz law, accounts for less than 8% of the total conductivity across the measured range, indicating that the anomaly is phononic in origin. We attribute the suppression to moiré-induced zone folding of the acoustic phonon branches, which opens minigaps on the order of 0.4 meV and introduces flat phonon bands that enhance umklapp scattering between hybridized modes. Temperature-dependent fits to a Callaway model with moiré-renormalized group velocities reproduce the measured conductivity without adjustable scattering parameters, supporting a picture in which phonon flat-band physics mirrors the electronic flat-band behavior characteristic of the magic angle.
fixtures.full_response:
<draft>
We report thermal conductivity measurements of twisted bilayer graphene at the magic angle (1.1°) from 10 K to 300 K using suspended microbridge thermometry. Near charge neutrality, the in-plane thermal conductivity is suppressed by a factor of 6.2 at 50 K relative to Bernal-stacked bilayer graphene, with the suppression persisting but weakening to a factor of 2.1 at 300 K. The electronic contribution, extracted via the Wiedemann-Franz law, accounts for less than 8% of the total conductivity across the measured range, indicating that the anomaly is phononic in origin. We attribute the suppression to moiré-induced zone folding of the acoustic phonon branches, which opens minigaps on the order of 0.4 meV and introduces flat phonon bands that enhance umklapp scattering between hybridized modes. Temperature-dependent fits to a Callaway model with moiré-renormalized group velocities reproduce the measured conductivity without adjustable scattering parameters, supporting a picture in which phonon flat-band physics mirrors the electronic flat-band behavior characteristic of the magic angle.
</draft>
